title: CSC_106 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: A browser opens `https://shop.ng:8080/cart?item=7&qty=2`. What are the port and the query string?
questions.concept: Parts of a URL: port and query
questions.why:
A URL reads scheme://host:port/path?query. After the host shop.ng comes :8080, so the port is 8080; after the ? comes the query string item=7&qty=2. The path is /cart.

443 is the default port for https, but this URL states 8080 explicitly; /cart is the path, not the query; 80 is the default for plain http and ?item=7 drops the second parameter.

questions.q: Which of these four is part of the Internet's infrastructure rather than an application running on top of it?
options: A fibre link between two ISPs' routers
A web page linked to another by a hyperlink
An email message waiting on a mail server
A chat app pushing messages to a phone
questions.why:
The Internet is the global network of interconnected computers and devices: cables, routers and links. Everything that sends data across it, including the Web, email and chat, is an application built on top of that infrastructure.

A hyperlinked web page is the World Wide Web, an application; an email message and a chat app are other applications carried by the Internet, not the wiring itself.

questions.q: You want to pause your JavaScript on a line and inspect which CSS rule turned a heading blue, without leaving the page you are viewing. Which tool category does this?
questions.concept: Matching a job to a web development tool category
questions.why:
Browser developer tools are built into the browser to inspect and manipulate page elements, debug JavaScript with breakpoints and analyse network traffic, all on the live page.

An IDE and a text editor edit code in files rather than inspecting the rendered page; a version control system tracks changes to code and has nothing to do with inspecting a running page.

questions.q: MongoDB, Nginx and Node.js. What type of server is each, in that order?
options: Web server, database server, application server
Database server, application server, web server
Database server, web server, application server
Application server, web server, database server
questions.concept: Identifying server types from example software
questions.why:
MongoDB stores and queries data, so it is a database server (with MySQL and PostgreSQL). Nginx serves web content and handles HTTP requests, so it is a web server (with Apache and Microsoft IIS). Node.js executes server-side application code, so it is an application server.

The other orders each swap two of the roles: Nginx is not a database, MongoDB is not a web server, and Node.js runs code rather than storing data.

questions.q: A developer builds a login feature on a private copy of the code for a week, then folds the finished work into the shared main line. Which version control capability is this?
questions.concept: Roles of a version control system
questions.why:
Working on a feature in isolation and then combining it with the main code line is branching (the isolated line of work) and merging (folding it back). Git is known for exactly this.

Code backup is keeping a safe copy of the repository; version history is the record of past commits you can compare or roll back to; load balancing is a server job, not a version control feature.

questions.q: A firm moves from every staff PC holding its own copy of the customer list to one server that holds the single list and answers every request for it. Which advantage of client-server architecture is this?
questions.why:
Holding the data in one place on the server, rather than scattered across clients, is centralised data management: one copy to update, secure and back up.

Separation of concerns is splitting interface work from server logic; scalability is adding servers to handle more clients; dynamic content generation is a server function, not one of the three architectural advantages.

questions.q: What does a web server do?
options: Stores web content and answers HTTP requests for it
Interprets HTML and draws the page on the screen
Translates domain names into IP addresses
Runs application code and manages user sessions
questions.why:
A web server is software or hardware that stores, manages and serves web content: it receives incoming HTTP requests, processes them and responds with the requested resources. Apache, Nginx and IIS are examples.

Interpreting HTML and drawing the page is the browser's job; translating names to IP addresses is DNS; running application code and managing sessions is an application server.

questions.q: What is an IDE, as distinct from a text editor?
options: A lightweight program for writing and editing code only
A browser panel for inspecting page elements
An environment bundling code editing with debugging and build tools
A system that tracks changes to code over time
questions.why:
An Integrated Development Environment such as WebStorm, Visual Studio or Eclipse provides code editing plus debugging, building and other development tooling in one place. A text editor such as VS Code, Sublime Text or Atom is lightweight and focused on editing.

The lightweight editing program is the text editor; the inspection panel is browser developer tools; tracking changes is a version control system.

questions.q: In the domain name `mail.students.unilag.edu.ng`, which label is the top-level domain, and is it a gTLD or a ccTLD?
questions.concept: DNS hierarchy: TLD, second-level domain, subdomain
questions.why:
Read a domain name from the right. The rightmost label is the top-level domain, here ng. Two-letter country codes such as .ng and .uk are country-code TLDs (ccTLDs); generic TLDs (gTLDs) are the likes of .com, .org and .net.

edu is the second-level domain under ng, not the TLD; ng is a country code so it is not generic; unilag is a subdomain of edu.ng, three labels from the right.

questions.q: A REST API keeps orders at `/orders`. Which request creates a new order?
questions.why:
REST maps HTTP methods onto CRUD: POST creates, GET retrieves, PUT updates, DELETE removes. Creating a new order is a POST to the collection /orders, with the order's details in the request body.

PUT updates an existing resource; GET only retrieves and never creates; CREATE is not an HTTP method.

questions.q: A student downloads email to a phone before boarding a bus with no signal, reads it offline, and the messages are no longer held on the server afterwards. Which retrieval protocol is in use?
questions.why:
POP3 downloads messages to the client device for offline access and typically removes them from the server. IMAP keeps messages on the server and synchronises actions across devices.

IMAP would have left the messages on the server; SMTP sends and relays outgoing mail, it does not retrieve; MIME is the message format standard for attachments and non-ASCII text, not a retrieval protocol.

questions.q: A mail server at miva.edu.ng must deliver a message to ade@unilag.edu.ng. Which DNS lookup tells it where to send the message?
options: A reverse DNS lookup of the sender's IP address
questions.why:
The Mail Exchanger (MX) record for a domain names the email servers that accept mail for it. The sending SMTP server looks up the MX record for unilag.edu.ng and connects to the server it names.

The A record for www gives the address of the website, not the mail server; a reverse lookup maps an IP address back to a name and says nothing about the recipient; the root and TLD servers only point down the hierarchy, they do not hold mail records.

questions.q: An attacker feeds a resolver a forged answer that points bank.ng at the attacker's own IP address (cache poisoning). Which mechanism lets the resolver reject the forgery, and how?
options: HTTPS; it encrypts the DNS query
DNSSEC; it adds digital signatures to DNS data
DNSSEC; it encrypts the DNS query
questions.why:
DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) adds digital signatures to DNS data so a resolver can verify that an answer is authentic and unaltered; a forged record fails the signature check, which prevents cache poisoning.

HTTPS secures web traffic, not DNS answers; DNSSEC signs rather than encrypts, so answers are authenticated but not hidden; SFTP is a secure file transfer protocol and plays no part in name resolution.

questions.q: A network capture of a login shows `POST /login` with `password=secret123` readable in plain text on port 80. Which protocol is in use, and what fixes the exposure?
options: HTTPS; the TLS certificate has expired
HTTP; send the form with GET instead
questions.why:
Port 80 with readable request text is plain HTTP, which has no built-in security: data travels in plaintext and can be intercepted. HTTPS adds encryption, so the same POST body is unreadable in transit.

HTTPS runs on port 443 and would not show readable text; FTP transfers files, not web forms; switching to GET would put the password in the URL as well, making things worse.

questions.q: Which markup language fits each job: (a) a logo that must stay sharp at any size, (b) a settings file using your own tag names, (c) a fraction displayed on a web page?
questions.concept: Choosing between HTML, XML, SVG, MathML and XHTML
questions.why:
SVG describes two-dimensional vector graphics that scale without losing quality, so it suits logos and icons. XML stores and exchanges structured data with user-defined tags, so it suits configuration files. MathML is the XML-based language for mathematical notation such as fractions.

XML does not draw graphics and XHTML is HTML made XML-strict, not a data format; HTML has a fixed tag set, so it cannot use your own tag names; MathML is for equations, not logos, and SVG does not typeset fractions.

questions.q: What is REST?
options: A protocol that exchanges strict XML messages between web services
A full-duplex channel kept open over a single TCP connection
A protocol for transferring files with encryption and authentication
An architectural style that is stateless and uses URLs with HTTP methods
questions.why:
REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style and set of constraints, not a protocol: resources are modelled as URLs, manipulated with GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, and each request is stateless, carrying everything the server needs.

Strict XML messages describe SOAP; a persistent full-duplex channel over one TCP connection is WebSocket; encrypted, authenticated file transfer is SFTP.

questions.q: A glossary must show the term HTML followed by its definition. Which markup is correct?
questions.concept: Definition list elements dl, dt, dd
questions.why:
A definition list is `<dl>` containing `<dt>` for each term and `<dd>` for its definition, in that order. So the term HTML goes in `<dt>` and the expansion in `<dd>`.

The first option swaps term and definition; `<ul>` is an unordered list and does not contain dt/dd; `<li>` is a list item for `<ol>` and `<ul>`, not for a definition list.

questions.q:
```html
<form action="/login" method="POST">
  <input type="text" name="user" value="ade">
  <input type="password" name="pw" value="x1">
  <button type="submit">Log in</button>
</form>
```
The user submits. Where do the two values travel?
options: In the body of a POST request to /login
questions.why:
With method="POST" the browser sends the form data in the request body of a POST to the action URL /login. Nothing appears in the address bar, which is why POST suits sensitive or large data.

Appending user=ade&pw=x1 to the URL is what method="GET" does; form data is never carried in the headers; POST moves data out of the URL but does not encrypt it, only HTTPS does that.

questions.q: A username box must accept no more than 8 characters. Which attribute on `<input type="text" name="user">` enforces this?
questions.why:
`maxlength` limits the number of characters that can be typed into a text input, so `maxlength="8"` is the attribute.

`max` limits the numeric value of a number input, not its length; `minlength` sets the fewest characters allowed; `pattern` takes a regular expression, and the pattern 8 would only accept the single character 8.

questions.q: A pizza form lists five toppings and the customer may pick any number of them, including none. Which input type is correct?
questions.why:
Checkboxes let the user select one or more options from a list, and none at all, which is what any-number-of-toppings needs.

Radio buttons in a group allow exactly one mutually exclusive choice; a plain `<select>` lets the user choose one option; a text input gives no list to pick from.

questions.q:
```html

Pay now or later.

``` How does this render?
options: now in italics, later in bold
now in bold, later in italics
now and later both in bold
questions.why:
`<strong>` marks strong importance and is displayed bold by default; `<em>` marks emphasis and is displayed in italics. So now is bold and later is italic.

Swapping them reverses the two elements; underlining comes from `<u>`, which is not used here; the two elements are different, so they do not both give bold.

questions.q: A page has, top to bottom: a bar with the site logo, a list of links to other pages, the main article text, and a copyright line. Which semantic elements hold each part, in order?
questions.why:
Semantic elements name the role of each part of the page: `<header>` for the introductory bar, `<nav>` for the navigation links, `<main>` for the principal content, `<footer>` for the closing copyright line. All sit inside `<body>`.

`<head>` holds invisible meta-information and is not the visible header; `<body>` is the container for everything visible, not one section; `<bottom>` and `<menu>`-as-navigation are not the semantic elements for these roles, and a bare `<ul>` carries no navigation meaning.

questions.q: Only the word sale in the sentence Big sale today must be styled differently, and the sentence must stay on one line. Which markup is correct?
questions.why:
`` is an inline container for styling part of the text inside a larger element, so wrapping just the word sale in a span keeps the sentence flowing on one line. `
` is a block container and would break the sentence onto separate lines; `

` inside `` is invalid nesting and `

questions.q: What is the purpose of the line `<!DOCTYPE html>` at the top of a page?
options: Tells the browser which HTML version to render with
Acts as the root element containing all others
questions.why:
The document type declaration is the first line of an HTML document and informs the browser which version of HTML is being used; for HTML5 it is exactly `<!DOCTYPE html>`, and it makes the browser render in standards mode.

Character encoding is declared by `<meta charset="UTF-8">`; the root element is `<html>`; the browser's default styles are built in and are not loaded by the DOCTYPE.

Total height = content + top/bottom padding + top/bottom border + top/bottom margin. `padding: 15px 30px` is 15px top and bottom (30px is left and right); `margin: 20px 0` is 20px top and bottom. So 120 + 15 + 15 + 3 + 3 + 20 + 20 = 196px.

156px forgets the margin; 226px uses the 30px horizontal padding for the vertical sides; 158px counts padding, border and margin on one side only.

questions.why:
`#intro` is an ID selector: it matches the single element whose id attribute is exactly intro, which is the paragraph A.

```html

questions.why:
`nav a` with a space is a descendant selector: it matches every `<a>` anywhere inside a `<nav>`, at any depth. One is a direct child and Two is nested inside ul and li, so both match.

options: Centred horizontally, sitting at the bottom
Centred vertically, pushed to the right
Centred horizontally, sitting at the top
Pushed to the left, centred vertically
questions.why:
With the default flex-direction: row the main axis is horizontal and the cross axis vertical. `justify-content: center` centres the items along the main axis (horizontally); `align-items: flex-end` places them at the end of the cross axis, the bottom of the 200px box.

Centred vertically and pushed right swaps the two axes; the top would be align-items: flex-start; pushed left and centred vertically is justify-content: flex-start with align-items: center.

questions.q:
```css
.row { display: flex; flex-direction: row-reverse; }
```
The .row contains A, B and C in that source order. Reading the screen from left to right, what appears?
options: A, B, C stacked top to bottom
C, B, A stacked top to bottom
questions.why:
`row-reverse` keeps the main axis horizontal but runs it right to left, so the first item A is placed at the right edge and C ends up leftmost: the screen reads C B A.

A B C is the default row; stacking top to bottom is column; stacked C, B, A from the top is column-reverse.

questions.q:
```css
html { font-size: 2vw; }
```
What is the root font size on a viewport 640px wide, and on one 1200px wide?
questions.why:
1vw is one hundredth of the viewport width, so 2vw is 2% of it: 0.02 × 640 = 12.8px and 0.02 × 1200 = 24px. The font scales with the screen, which is fluid typography.

20px; 20px treats the value as fixed, which is what px would give; 6.4px; 12px uses 1vw instead of 2vw; 32px; 60px uses 5vw.

questions.q:
```html

web tech basics

``` ```css .t { text-transform: capitalize; text-decoration: line-through; } ``` How does the text render?
options: Every letter upper case, with a line through the text
First letter of each word capitalised, with a line through the text
First letter of each word capitalised, with the text underlined
Text left exactly as typed, with a line through it
questions.why:
`text-transform: capitalize` upper-cases the first letter of every word, turning web tech basics into Web Tech Basics; `text-decoration: line-through` draws a line through that text.

Every letter upper case is text-transform: uppercase; underlining is text-decoration: underline, not line-through; text left as typed would mean no text-transform at all, but capitalize does change it.

questions.q:
```html AB
C
D
``` With default styles, how many lines does this occupy, and what is on each?
options: One line: A B C D
Three lines: A B together, then C, then D
Four lines: A, B, C, D each on its own
Two lines: A on one, B C D on the other
questions.why:
`<span>` is inline: it takes only the width it needs and does not start a new line, so A and B share a line. `<div>` is block: each fills the parent's width and starts on a new line, so C and D each get their own. That is three lines.

One line would need every element inline; four lines treats spans as block; two lines gets the split backwards.

questions.q: What is the difference between padding and margin?
options: Padding is the space inside the border; margin is the space outside it
Padding is the space outside the border; margin is the space inside it
Padding sets the border's thickness; margin sets the content width
Both sit inside the border; margin is simply the larger of the two
questions.concept: Padding versus margin in the box model
questions.why:
In the box model the layers from the inside out are content, padding, border, margin. Padding is the space between the content and the border, and the element's background extends into it; margin is the space outside the border that separates the element from its neighbours.

The second option reverses the two; border thickness is border-width and content width is width; margin is never inside the border.

questions.concept: Block scope of let versus var
questions.why:
`var` is not block-scoped, so a is still visible after the if block and typeof a is number. `let` is block-scoped, so b does not exist outside the braces; typeof on an undeclared name does not throw, it returns undefined. Output: number undefined.

number number would need both to escape the block; undefined undefined would need var to be block-scoped too; typeof never throws a ReferenceError for an undeclared name, though `console.log(b)` would.

7 % 2 is 1, so `n % 2 === 0` is false and the first ternary takes its else branch, which is another ternary: 7 > 5 is true, giving "big odd".

even would need 7 % 2 to be 0; small odd would need n ≤ 5; true is the value of the comparison, but the ternary returns one of the two strings, not the condition.

A do-while checks its condition after the body, so the body runs once: count becomes 1 and i becomes 11. Then 11 < 5 is false and the loop stops. Output: 1 11.

0 10 is what a plain while loop would give, since 10 < 5 is false from the start; 5 15 assumes the loop ran until i reached 15; 1 10 forgets that i++ ran in the body.

sq is an arrow function returning x squared; f is a function expression. f(3, 4) computes sq(3) + 4 = 9 + 4 = 13. A function's typeof is "function". Output: 13 function.

49 squares a + b instead of a alone; object is wrong because functions report typeof function; 7 adds 3 and 4 without squaring.

questions.concept: Nested arrays and the length property
questions.why:
m holds two inner arrays, so m.length is 2. m[1] is [4, 5], length 2. m[0][2] is 3 (zero-indexed third element of the first row) and m[1][0] is 4, so the sum is 7. Output: 2 2 7.

5 2 7 counts every number instead of the two rows; 2 3 7 reads the length of the first row instead of the second; 2 2 34 concatenates as strings, but these are numbers so + adds.

new Student creates an object with two properties, name and score. `s.score += 15` changes score to 85; `s["level"] = 200` adds a third property using square-bracket notation. So there are 3 keys and score is 85.

2 85 forgets that assigning to a new key adds a property; 3 70 forgets the += 15; 7015 would be string concatenation, but score is a number.

area is a method; inside it `this` refers to box, so it reads the current values of w and h when called. w was changed to 6 before the call, so 6 × 5 = 30.

20 uses the original w of 4; 11 adds instead of multiplies; function would be the result of logging box.area without the parentheses that call it.

With a string operand, + concatenates: "10" + 5 is "105". The other arithmetic operators convert the string to a number: "10" - 5 is 5 and "10" * 2 is 20, and the result of subtraction is a number. Output: 105 5 20 number.

15 treats + as numeric addition; string is wrong because - always produces a number; NaN would only arise if "10" could not be converted to a number.

questions.q: What does `===` check that `==` does not?
options: That the two values are equal after rounding
That the data types match as well as the values
That both variables point to the same object
questions.why:
`==` compares values after converting types, so 5 == "5" is true. `===` is strict equality: the values must be equal and of the same data type, so 5 === "5" is false.

Neither operator rounds; both work on any types, not only numbers; identity of objects is checked by both operators alike, the difference is type conversion.

Destructuring pulls name ("Ada") out of the object and, from the marks array, the first element into first (60). The template literal, written with backticks, evaluates each ${} expression: first + 5 is 65. Output: Ada: 65.

The literal ${...} text would appear only with ordinary quotes instead of backticks; 605 would need string concatenation, but first is a number; 60 forgets the + 5.

options: The message appears and the form is not sent
The form is sent and then the message appears
The page reloads and no message is shown
An error is thrown because value is undefined
questions.why:
The submit listener runs first. An empty input has value "", so the condition is true, e.preventDefault() cancels the browser's default action of submitting the form, and the message text is written into the page. The form is not sent.

Once preventDefault runs the form is not submitted at all; a reload is what would happen without preventDefault; an input's value is always a string, never undefined, so no error is thrown.

Calling run() executes synchronously up to the first await, so 1 prints. await hands control back and the rest of run is queued as a microtask; the caller continues and prints 3. When the synchronous code finishes the microtask runs and prints 2. Order: 1 3 2.

1 2 3 assumes await does not pause; 3 1 2 assumes an async function starts later, but its body runs immediately until the first await; 2 is not skipped, it is only deferred.

questions.q:
What does this print?

```js
Promise.reject(new Error("bad"))
  .then(() => console.log("A"))
  .catch(e => { console.log("B"); return 1; })
  .then(v => console.log("C", v));
```
questions.why:
The promise starts rejected, so the first .then is skipped and control jumps to .catch, which prints B and returns 1. Returning a value from catch produces a fulfilled promise, so the final .then runs with v = 1 and prints C 1.

A never prints because a .then handler does not run on a rejected promise; B alone forgets that catch recovers the chain; A C 1 ignores the rejection.

In the call, ...arr spreads the array into separate arguments, so count receives 1, 2, 3, 4: first is 1 and the rest parameter gathers [2, 3, 4], length 3. In count(arr) the whole array is one argument, so first is the array and rest is empty, length 0. Output: 3 0.

4 counts first as well as the rest; 1 for the second call treats the single array argument as if it were spread into rest.

options: First paragraph shows New in bold type; second is unchanged
First paragraph shows the literal text New; second unchanged
Both paragraphs show New in bold
questions.why: querySelector returns only the first element matching the selector, so el is the paragraph Old. textContent sets plain text, not markup, so the tags are displayed literally as New. setAttribute adds id="first" but changes nothing visible. The second paragraph is untouched. Bold rendering would need innerHTML, which parses markup; both paragraphs would change only with querySelectorAll and a loop.

questions.q: What is a promise in JavaScript?
options: A function passed as an argument to run when a task finishes
An object standing for a value that will arrive later
A keyword that pauses a function until an operation completes
The queue the event loop empties before running timers
questions.why:
A promise is an object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation; it is pending until it is either fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason, and you attach handlers with .then() and .catch().

A function passed in to run later is a callback; the keyword that pauses an async function is await; the queue drained before timers is the microtask queue, where promise callbacks wait.

questions.q: What is the difference between XSS and CSRF?
options: XSS injects script into your page; CSRF makes a logged-in user's browser send an unwanted request
XSS makes a logged-in user's browser send an unwanted request; CSRF injects script into your page
XSS steals passwords in transit; CSRF forges DNS answers
XSS is a client-side validation error; CSRF is a server-side validation error
questions.why:
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) gets attacker-supplied code to run inside your page, which is why user input should be written with textContent rather than innerHTML. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tricks a user's browser into sending a request to your site using their existing session, defended with anti-CSRF tokens.

The second option swaps the two; interception in transit is the HTTP-versus-HTTPS problem and forged DNS answers are cache poisoning; neither attack is a validation error.

getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection that updates as the document changes, so after appendChild it holds 3 elements. querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList, a snapshot taken at the moment of the call, so it stays at 2. Logged: 3 2.

2 2 treats both as snapshots; 3 3 treats both as live; 2 3 swaps the two results.

questions.q:
```html

``` ```js document.getElementById("one").textContent = "Sale"; document.getElementById("two").innerHTML = "Sale"; ``` What do the two paragraphs show on the page?
options: Sale in italics, then the characters Sale
The characters Sale, then Sale in italics
questions.why: textContent writes plain text, so the tags are escaped and appear on screen as the characters Sale. innerHTML writes parsed markup, so the tag becomes a real element and Sale is rendered in italics. The second option swaps the two properties; the last two assume both behave alike. Only innerHTML parses what you assign, which is why assigning untrusted input to it is the cross site scripting risk.

questions.why:
querySelectorAll takes a CSS selector and returns a NodeList of every match, so index 1 is the second list item.

questions.why:

```html

questions.why:
A data- attribute is read through dataset with the hyphenated name turned into camelCase, so data-task-id is dataset.taskId. Every dataset value is a string, so typeof gives "string", and the string "false" is not strictly equal to the boolean false. Logged: string false.

number false and boolean true assume the browser converts the value to a number or a boolean; string true assumes "false" equals false, which strict equality rejects because the types differ.

bump() with parentheses runs the function immediately, so n becomes 2 while the listener is being registered, and what gets registered is bump's return value, undefined. The two clicks therefore do nothing and n stays 2.

4 counts the two clicks but not the immediate call; 6 counts all three; 0 assumes nothing ran at all. The correct registration passes the name with no parentheses: addEventListener("click", bump).

questions.why:
children counts element nodes only, so it is 2. childNodes counts every node, and the line breaks and indentation between the tags are text nodes: text, element, text, element, text gives 5. Logged: 2 5.

questions.concept: Element nodes versus all child nodes

questions.why:
Each image gets its own click listener, and the handler writes that image's alt text into the caption. Assigning to textContent replaces the whole content, so the second click writes Lagos over Abuja and the div reads Lagos.

Abuja is the state after the first click only. The two joined answers assume textContent appends, which it never does.
questions.concept: One handler attached to many elements

questions.q: What is the difference between an element node and a text node in a DOM tree?
options: An element node is a tag; a text node is the value of an attribute
An element node holds only text; a text node holds child tags
An element node comes from the HTML; a text node is created only by JavaScript
An element node is a tag; a text node is the character data inside an element
questions.why:
Everything in a DOM tree is a node. Element nodes are the tags such as
,

and ; text nodes are the character data inside an element, such as "Read more"; attribute nodes are the attributes on a tag, such as src or href. An attribute value is an attribute node, not a text node. Elements contain text nodes rather than being made of text, and text nodes exist as soon as the browser parses the HTML, with or without any script.

questions.q:
jQuery is loaded and the page is: ```html

A

B

C

``` ```js $("p.note").css("color", "red").text("Read this"); ``` What is the result?
options: All three paragraphs turn red and read Read this
Nothing changes, because .text() cannot be chained after .css()
Both note paragraphs turn red and read Read this
Only the first note paragraph turns red and reads Read this
questions.why:
A jQuery selector returns every element that matches, and a method called on that set applies to all of them, then returns the set again, which is what makes chaining work. Both paragraphs carrying class note turn red and have their text replaced.

Acting on the first match only is querySelector behaviour, not jQuery. The plain paragraph does not carry the class, so it is untouched. Chaining is a normal jQuery feature, so the last option is wrong.
questions.concept: jQuery acts on every matched element

questions.q:
```js
const r = _.chain([4, 1, 4, 3, 1]).uniq().sortBy().value();
```
Lodash is loaded. What is `r`?
questions.why:
uniq drops repeated values, leaving [4, 1, 3]; sortBy then orders them ascending; value() ends the chain and returns the result, [1, 3, 4].

[4, 1, 3] stops after uniq and forgets the sort; [1, 1, 3, 4, 4] sorts without removing duplicates; [4, 3, 1] sorts in the wrong direction.
questions.concept: Lodash method chaining over an array

questions.q: A booking page must turn a stored date into "Monday, 26 October 2026", shift it to the user's timezone and print the month name in the user's language. Which library is built for this?
questions.why:
Moment.js parses, formats and does arithmetic on dates and times, with timezone and locale support, which is exactly what is needed here.

Lodash works on arrays, objects and strings held in memory. jQuery works on the document: selection, events, AJAX and animation. Express.js is a Node.js backend framework, not a browser library.
questions.concept: Matching a task to the right JavaScript library

questions.q: In one framework, typing in a text box updates the data model with no extra code written, and changing the model in code updates the text box. Which feature is this?
questions.why:
Two way data binding, the Angular feature, keeps the user interface and the data model synchronised in both directions, so a change to either affects the other.

Unidirectional data flow is React's model, where data passes from parent to child only. The virtual DOM is React's in memory copy, diffed so that only changed parts of the page are updated. Dependency injection supplies service instances to a component, a different Angular feature.
questions.concept: Two way data binding versus unidirectional data flow

questions.why:
Middleware runs in the order it is defined. The first sets a header and calls next(), so the chain continues. The second sends a 401 response and never calls next(), so the route handler is never reached and the body is Denied.

Report assumes a route always wins over middleware. DeniedReport assumes both run, but one request gets one response. The last option ignores the status the answering middleware set.
questions.concept: Middleware order in the request cycle

questions.q: A team must build an internal data entry site in Python and wants a generated admin panel plus user login and permissions without writing them. Which framework fits?
questions.why:
Django is the Python framework named for the admin interface it generates and for built in authentication and authorization, so both requirements are met out of the box.

Express.js is minimal and middleware based, so those features are assembled by hand, and it runs on Node.js rather than Python. Ruby on Rails is Ruby, known for convention over configuration and Active Record. ASP.NET is C# in the Microsoft ecosystem.
questions.concept: Choosing a backend framework from its features

questions.q: What is middleware in Express.js?
options: A layer that maps model classes onto database tables
Functions with access to the request and response objects that run in the order defined, before the route handler
The rule that decides which handler answers an incoming URL
A template engine that builds HTML on the server before it is sent
questions.why:
Middleware functions sit inside the request and response cycle, have access to the request and response objects, and execute in the order they are defined, forming a pipeline used for authentication, logging and parsing before the route handler runs.

Deciding which handler answers a URL is routing. Building HTML on the server is the job of a template engine such as EJS or Handlebars. Mapping model classes onto tables is an object relational mapper, for example Active Record.

questions.q: Vue.js is described as a progressive framework. What does that mean?
options: It replaces the browser DOM with a copy that it diffs on every change
It requires the whole application to be rewritten in its own module system
It can be adopted incrementally, from one part of a page up to a whole application
It compiles the application to a binary format before the browser runs it
questions.why:
Vue focuses on the view layer and is incrementally adoptable: you use as much or as little of it as you need, dropping it into one page of an existing site or growing it into a full application. That, with its gentle learning curve, is why it is called progressive.

Compiling to a binary describes WebAssembly. Diffing an in memory copy of the page describes React's virtual DOM. Expecting to own the whole application describes Angular.
questions.concept: Vue as a progressive, incrementally adoptable framework

questions.why:
In PHP the plus sign is arithmetic only, so the numeric string "5" is converted and "5" + 3 gives 8. The dot is the concatenation operator, so "5" . 3 joins them into the string 53. Printed: 8 53.

53 53 treats plus as string joining, the habit carried over from JavaScript; 8 8 treats the dot as addition; 53 8 swaps the two operators.

+= adds and assigns, so $total becomes 27. %= takes the remainder and assigns, and 27 divided by 4 is 6 remainder 3, so $total ends at 3.

6 gives the quotient rather than the remainder; 7 applies the modulus before the addition, 20 % 4 then plus 7; 6.75 uses division instead of modulus.
questions.concept: Compound assignment and the modulus operator

questions.why:
The loop runs with i from 1 to 6 inclusive. The condition is true for the even values 2, 4 and 6, and .= appends each one to the string, giving 246.

135 keeps the values whose remainder is 1, so it tests the wrong condition; 24 stops at 4, an off by one that ends the loop while i is under 6; 123456 appends every value and ignores the condition.
questions.concept: Building a string in a for loop

questions.why:
17 >= 18 is false, so the first ternary yields the value after the colon, 250. Then 250 > 300 is false, so the second yields concession. Printed: 250 concession.

500 full takes the true branch of both tests. The two mixed answers take the true branch of one and the false branch of the other, which is what happens if the ternary is read as condition ? false value : true value.

The $rate written inside the function is a local variable, separate from the global one, so total(10) multiplies by 2 and returns 20. That assignment never touches the global $rate, which is still 5. Printed: 20 5.

50 5 assumes the function can see the global value; 20 2 assumes the local assignment overwrote the global; 50 2 makes both mistakes together.

twice echoes 8 the moment it is called, before the bar is printed. It has no return statement, so it hands back NULL, and echoing NULL prints nothing. Printed: 8|.

|8 assumes the value appears only at the end; 8|8 assumes the function both echoes and returns 8; 8|0 assumes a missing return gives 0, but the absent value is NULL, which prints as an empty string.
questions.concept: Returning a value versus echoing it

questions.why:
Each call joins its own $n in front of the result of the call below it, so the digits come out from 4 downwards, and the base case at 0 contributes the empty string: 4321.

1234 reverses the order, which is what you get by joining after the recursive call instead of before it; 43210 counts the base case as the character 0; 432 stops the recursion at 1 rather than 0.

questions.q:
```php

``` What does the browser receive?
options:
The `

questions.why:
PHP runs on the server and only its output travels to the browser. $stock is 0, so the condition is false and the else branch echoes Sold out inside the paragraph, giving

In stock

questions.concept: PHP executing on the server before HTML is sent

questions.q: In PHP, what is the difference between `=` and `==`?
options: `=` assigns a value to a variable; `==` compares two values and gives a boolean
`=` compares two values; `==` assigns a value to a variable
`=` compares values only; `==` compares values and data types
`=` joins two strings; `==` adds two numbers
questions.why:
The single equals sign is the assignment operator: it puts the value on its right into the variable on its left. The double equals sign is a comparison operator: it tests whether two values are equal and returns true or false.

The second option reverses them, which is the mistake behind writing if ($x = 5), a line that assigns rather than compares. The third describes the difference between == and ===. The fourth describes the dot and the plus.

questions.q: A mobile app must fetch the profile of user 77 from an API that keeps users at `/api/users`, without changing anything. Which request does it send?
questions.why:
GET is the method whose job is to retrieve data and change nothing, and a single user is one resource, addressed by adding its id to the collection path.

POST creates data, normally sent to the collection endpoint. GET /api/users returns the whole collection instead of the one profile. PUT updates the resource at that address, so it changes data the app was told to leave alone.
questions.concept: Choosing an HTTP method and endpoint

questions.q: An API endpoint requires a token. A client calls it with no token at all. Which status code should the response carry?
questions.why:
401 is the client error code for a request that has not been authenticated, which is exactly what a missing token means.

404 says the endpoint or resource was not found; 429 says the client has passed its rate limit; 500 says the server itself failed while processing an otherwise valid request. The status is the part of the response the client checks before reading the body.
questions.concept: Matching an API failure to its status code

questions.q: A dashboard must hold about 20,000 open connections and push each price change out the moment it arrives. Which server side language is chosen for this, and for what reason?
options: Node.js, for its event driven, non blocking I/O
Java, for its reliability and scalability
PHP, for its simplicity and embedding in HTML
questions.why:
Node.js runs JavaScript on the server with an event driven, non blocking I/O model, so a slow operation does not stall the process and one server can hold a large number of concurrent connections. That is the stated reason it suits real time applications.

The other three name each language with the quality it is known for, but reliability, simplicity and elegant syntax are not what makes thousands of live connections cheap to keep open.
questions.concept: Matching a server side language to a workload

questions.q: A web server environment is listed as Ubuntu Server, Apache, MySQL and PHP, managed with phpMyAdmin and Fail2ban. Which stack is this, and which component is the operating system?
questions.why:
LAMP stands for Linux, Apache, MySQL and PHP, and Ubuntu Server is the Linux distribution, so it is the operating system component of the environment.

Apache is the web server and MySQL is the database server; both are server software sitting on top of the operating system. MEAN names a different stack altogether, built on MongoDB, Express, Angular and Node.js.

questions.q: A query that filters `orders` on `customer_id` reads every row and takes 4 seconds. The data is already split cleanly across related tables. Which technique fixes the speed?
questions.why:
An index is a structure built on a frequently queried column so the database can find matching rows without scanning the whole table, which is the standard cure for a slow filter.

Normalization splits data across related tables to cut redundancy and improve integrity, and the data is already normalised, so further splitting would not help and can slow reads. More application servers do not change how the database finds rows. Allowing NULL changes what may be stored, not how it is searched.

questions.q: A catalogue holds millions of product records whose fields differ from one supplier to the next, with no fixed set of columns. Which database management system suits it?
questions.why:
MongoDB is the NoSQL, document oriented and schema less system meant for large volumes of unstructured or semi structured data with flexible data models, which is what records with varying fields are.

MySQL and Oracle Database are relational systems with a fixed schema of tables and columns. Redis is NoSQL too, but it is an in memory key value store for caching, real time analytics and message brokering, not a store for millions of catalogue records.
questions.concept: Choosing SQL or NoSQL for a data shape

questions.q: What is a database management system?
options: Software that provides an interface for storing, retrieving, manipulating and securing data in databases
A structured collection of data organised for efficient storage and retrieval
The blueprint of the tables, fields, data types and relationships of one database
A domain specific language for querying and managing relational databases
questions.why:
A database management system is the software layer you interact with: it manages storage, retrieval, manipulation, user access and security for the databases it holds. MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB are examples.

The second option defines a database itself, the data rather than the software. The third defines a schema. The fourth defines SQL, the language you send to the system.
questions.concept: Database, DBMS, schema and SQL distinguished

questions.q: What is the difference between a data model and a schema?
options: A data model is an index on a column; a schema is a backup copy of the tables
A data model is the conceptual structure of data; a schema is one database's concrete blueprint
A data model is one database's concrete blueprint; a schema is the conceptual structure of data
A data model is the software that manages the data; a schema is the language used to query it
questions.why:
A data model is the conceptual representation of how data is structured and related, and relational, document and graph are the three named models. A schema is the concrete blueprint of one database: its tables, fields, data types and relationships.

The second option swaps them. The third describes a database management system and SQL. MongoDB being schema less still has a data model, the document model, which shows the two terms are not interchangeable.

questions.q:
```php
$sql = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = " . $_GET["id"];
```
Which change removes the injection risk on this line?
options: Encode the query result before printing it to the page
Send the id in a POST body instead of the query string
Use a prepared statement with a placeholder for the id
Wrap the value in double quotes before joining it
questions.why:
The value from the request is pasted straight into the SQL text, so a crafted id changes what the query means. A prepared statement sends the query and the value separately, so the value can never be read as SQL. Input validation and parameterised queries are the named defence against SQL injection.

Quoting can be broken by the attacker's own quote character. Encoding output defends against cross site scripting instead. Moving the value into a POST body changes only where it travels; it is still user input pasted into SQL.
questions.concept: Preventing SQL injection with parameterised queries

questions.q: A site now encodes everything it prints from user input and adds a Content Security Policy that refuses to run inline scripts. Which vulnerability is being closed?
questions.why:
Cross site scripting is a malicious script injected into a page that other users then view. Output encoding and a Content Security Policy are its two named mitigations.

SQL injection is closed by input validation and parameterised queries. Cross site request forgery is closed by unique session tokens and session expiration. Security misconfiguration is closed by correcting the settings themselves, such as turning off debug output on a live site.
questions.concept: Matching a defence to the vulnerability it closes

questions.q: A login form now asks for a one time code from an authenticator app as well as the password. Which practice is this, and which property does it strengthen?
questions.why:
Asking for a second proof of identity is two factor authentication, and authentication is the step that verifies who the user is.

Authorisation is the separate step that decides what an identified user may do, through roles and permissions, and a second factor changes none of those privileges. Session management means unique tokens and expiry; security headers are response headers such as HSTS and X-Content-Type-Options.

questions.q: Requests carrying `' OR 1=1--` in a form field are inspected and blocked before they reach the application code at all. Which component did that?
questions.why:
A web application firewall filters and monitors HTTP and HTTPS requests, recognises malicious patterns and payloads, and blocks them before they reach the application. It is an additional layer rather than a replacement for secure coding.

A load balancer spreads traffic across servers. A content delivery network caches content near users. A version control system keeps a history of code. None of the three inspects request payloads for attacks.
questions.concept: What a web application firewall does

questions.q: Visitors in Nairobi wait about 900 ms for images served from a single server in London, while that server is barely loaded. Which fix cuts the wait most directly?
options: Upgrade the London server's CPU and memory
Add an index to the products table
Move the site to shared hosting
Serve the images from a content delivery network
questions.why:
The delay comes from the distance between the users and the single server. A content delivery network is a geographically distributed set of servers that cache content and deliver it from a location close to the user, which is what cuts latency here.

Upgrading the server is vertical scaling and shortens no network path, and the server is not the bottleneck. A database index speeds up queries, not image delivery. Shared hosting is the cheapest option with limited performance, so it would make matters worse.
questions.concept: Latency from distance and the CDN fix

questions.q: One application server handles at most 250 concurrent users. Peak demand is 1,100 concurrent users, and the team wants one spare identical server so peak is still met if one fails. How many servers do they run?
questions.why:
1,100 divided by 250 is 4.4, and a server cannot be a fraction, so 5 are needed to carry the peak. One spare for failover makes 6.

5 meets peak with no spare left over; 4 rounds 4.4 down and falls 100 users short; 7 adds two spares rather than one. Adding machines behind a load balancer like this is horizontal scaling, as against vertical scaling, which upgrades a single machine.

questions.q: A rule sends the on call engineer a notification whenever CPU use stays above 90 percent for five minutes. Which monitoring concept is this?
questions.why:
An alert fires when a monitored value crosses a threshold, which is precisely a notification triggered by CPU staying above 90 percent for five minutes.

Metrics are the measurements themselves, such as response times, error rates and resource use; the CPU figure is the metric and the notification is the alert. Logging is the recorded history of events, actions and errors. Error handling, with try and catch, belongs to debugging rather than monitoring.

questions.q: What is the difference between deployment and hosting?
options: Deployment provides the infrastructure that makes a site reachable; hosting sets up and configures the servers
Deployment is writing the application code; hosting is testing it before release
Deployment means adding more servers; hosting means upgrading the existing one
Deployment sets up and configures the servers; hosting provides the infrastructure that makes the site reachable
questions.why:
Deployment is the work of setting up and configuring servers, covering their hardware, software and network. Hosting is the service that provides the resources and infrastructure that make the application reachable over the internet.

The second option swaps the two. The third describes development and testing. The fourth describes horizontal and vertical scaling.

questions.q: A physics engine written in C++ must run inside the browser at close to native speed. What is the C++ compiled to?
options: A service worker that runs in the background
WebAssembly, a binary instruction format the browser executes
Minified JavaScript, which the browser interprets
A JSON bundle that the page loads and parses
questions.why:
WebAssembly is a binary instruction format designed for web browsers. Code written in C++, Rust or TypeScript is compiled into it and the browser executes it directly at near native speed, which is why it suits gaming, simulations and video editing.

JavaScript is interpreted, and its performance limits are what WebAssembly exists to address. JSON is a data format, not executable code. A service worker is the background script behind offline access and push notifications in a progressive web app.
questions.concept: What WebAssembly is and where it comes from

questions.q: Untrusted third party code is run in the browser as WebAssembly and cannot reach the user's files or other pages. Which named advantage of WebAssembly is this?
options: Security, from running in a sandboxed environment
Speed and performance close to native code
Cross platform compatibility across major browsers
questions.why:
WebAssembly executes in a sandboxed environment isolated from the rest of the system, and running untrusted code safely is the example given for its security advantage.

Speed and performance is the near native execution advantage. Cross platform compatibility is one build running in all major browsers, on desktop and mobile. Progressive enhancement is a progressive web app principle, not a WebAssembly advantage at all.

questions.q: The first call to a serverless function after an idle hour takes 2.5 seconds, while the calls that follow take about 40 ms each. Which serverless challenge is this?
questions.why:
A cold start is the delay while the provider brings up a new instance for a function that has not run recently; once it is warm the following calls are quick. Cold starts and vendor lock in are the two named challenges of serverless architecture.

Vendor lock in is the difficulty of moving to another provider. Statelessness means no state is kept between invocations, which does not on its own make the first call slow. Rate limiting caps how many requests a client may send.
questions.concept: The named challenges of serverless architecture

questions.q: A retailer feeds 50,000 unlabelled purchase histories to a model and it groups the shoppers into six segments that nobody defined in advance. Which type of machine learning is this?
questions.why:
Unsupervised learning trains on unlabelled data to find patterns and groupings, and clustering customers into market segments is its named example. Clustering is always unsupervised.

Supervised learning needs labelled data, as a spam filter trained on mail already marked spam or not spam does. Natural language processing works on human language and computer vision on images and video; neither names a learning style.

questions.q: A support tool reads a customer's typed complaint, works out what is being asked and answers in plain English. Which field of artificial intelligence is this?
questions.why:
Natural language processing is computers understanding, interpreting and generating human language, and a chatbot answering user queries is its named example.

Computer vision interprets visual information from images and video, such as facial recognition. Deep learning names a technique, neural networks with many layers, rather than the task. Edge artificial intelligence means running models close to where the data is generated, for low latency.

questions.q: Every menu, button and form field on a site can be reached and activated with the keyboard alone. Which accessibility principle does this satisfy?
questions.why:
Operable means the interface can be navigated and used through various inputs, and the named example is that all interactive elements are keyboard accessible.

Perceivable is about users being able to sense the content, with alternative text for images as its example. Understandable is about clear content and plain language. Robust is about working with current and future technologies, with semantic HTML as its example.

questions.q: A news app opened from the phone's home screen still shows yesterday's articles in flight mode, and it can deliver push notifications. Which technology provides both?
questions.why:
Service workers are the scripts behind a progressive web app's offline access, caching of resources for faster loading, and push notifications, which covers both behaviours described.

Responsive design adapts the layout to screen size and orientation. Two way data binding is an Angular feature for keeping a model and a form field in step. A load balancer distributes traffic between servers and has nothing to do with a device being offline.
questions.concept: What service workers give a progressive web app

questions.q: What is the difference between web accessibility and inclusivity?
options: Accessibility makes content usable by people with disabilities; inclusivity designs for all users regardless of ability
Accessibility designs for all users regardless of ability; inclusivity makes content usable by people with disabilities
Accessibility applies to mobile devices; inclusivity applies to desktop computers
Accessibility is a set of testing tools; inclusivity is a legal requirement
questions.why:
Web accessibility is ensuring that sites, applications and content are usable by people with disabilities, covering visual, auditory, motor and cognitive needs. Inclusivity goes further, designing for all users regardless of ability.

The second option swaps the two. Neither term is about a class of device, and neither is only a toolset or only a legal duty, although regulations such as the Americans with Disabilities Act do apply to accessibility.
